t.3.68.1: Bṛhadaśva said: Then, after a long time, a brahmin named Parṇāda returned to the city and spoke these words to Bhaimī.
t.3.68.3: And I made the illustrious Ṛtuparṇa hear your message in the great assembly, just as it was spoken, O lady of fair complexion.
t.3.68.2: O Damayantī, as I searched day and night for the Naiṣadha, I went to the city of Ayodhyā, and Bhāṅgasvari was approached by me.
t.3.68.4: Hearing that, King Ṛtuparṇa said nothing, nor did any member of his assembly, though I addressed them again and again.
t.3.68.5: But when I had taken leave of the king, someone spoke to me in a lonely place: a man of Ṛtuparṇa's, Bāhuka by name.
t.3.68.6: The charioteer of that king is misshapen and short-armed, highly skilled in swift driving, and a maker of delicious dishes in the preparation of food.
t.3.68.7: He sighed many times and wept again and again, and after asking me about my welfare, he afterwards said this.
t.3.68.8: Even when they have fallen into adversity, women of noble family guard themselves by themselves; such virtuous women have won heaven, there is no doubt. And even when abandoned by their husbands, they never grow angry.
t.3.68.10: The dark-skinned lady ought not to be angry with one who was seeking the bare means of keeping alive, whose garment was carried off by birds, and who was being consumed by anguish.
t.3.68.9: That she was abandoned by him, who was in dire straits, bewildered, and bereft of happiness, she ought not to be angry at that.
t.3.68.11: Whether she be honored or dishonored, the dark-complexioned lady, seeing her husband in such a plight, bereft of his kingdom and stripped of his fortune, ought not to be angry.
t.3.68.13: Having heard this from Parṇāda, O lord of the people, Damayantī, her eyes filled with tears, went to her mother in private and spoke to her.
t.3.68.12: Having heard those words of his, I have come here in haste. Now that you have heard it, you are the judge; and make it known to the king as well.
t.3.68.14: This matter must by no means be made known to Bhīma, mother. In your presence I shall instruct Sudeva, the best of the twice-born.
t.3.68.15: You must strive so that King Bhīma does not come to know of my intention, if you wish to do what is dear to me.
t.3.68.16: And just as I was swiftly brought back to my kinsmen by Sudeva, so by that same auspicious means, mother, let Sudeva go quickly, without delay, from here to the city of Ayodhyā to bring back Nala.
t.3.68.17: And then afterwards, when Parṇāda, the best of brahmins, had rested, the beautiful Vaidarbhī honored him lavishly with wealth.
t.3.68.18: And when Nala has come here, O brahmin, I shall give you still more wealth, for you have done much for me, as no other will do, in that I shall soon be reunited with my husband, O best of the twice-born.
t.3.68.19: Thus addressed, that high-minded man honored her with most auspicious blessings, and then, his purpose accomplished, he went home.
t.3.68.20: Then, O Yudhiṣṭhira, Damayantī, filled with pain and grief, had that brahmin brought to her and spoke to him in the presence of her mother.
t.3.68.21: Go, Sudeva, to the city, and speak these words to King Ṛtuparṇa, who dwells in Ayodhyā: "Wishing to choose another husband, Damayantī, the daughter of Bhīma, will once again hold a svayaṃvara."
t.3.68.22: Kings and princes from every quarter are going there, and as the time has been reckoned, it will take place when tomorrow has dawned.
t.3.68.23: If it seems possible to you, go quickly, O tamer of foes, for at sunrise she will choose a second husband, since it is not known whether the hero Nala is living or dead.
t.3.68.24: Then, O great king, the brahmin Sudeva went to King Ṛtuparṇa and spoke to him just as she had instructed.
